children: The average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a fresh record high of $6.27 on Tuesday, according to the American Automobile Association.
U.S. diesel prices are soaring once again as the squeeze in the fuels market tightens, breaching $6 a gallon for the first time on Friday.
Prices had jumped at the start of the conflict before cooling after refiners ramped up production. The average price for a gallon of diesel was $3.69 a year ago.

The higher prices are a blow to President Trump who made easing the cost of living central to his 2024 reelection campaign and has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. However, energy-cost inflation has boosted expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates Wednesday.
In California, the average price of diesel was at $8.21 a gallon, the AAA said Tuesday.

The administration has tried to increase the country's fuel-making capacity while playing down persistent speculation that it is seriously weighing a temporary ban on U.S. exports of refined products such as diesel.

Any ban is unlikely to lower prices over the long run. It could offer some immediate relief but would eventually weigh on refinery margins and lead to refiners cutting run rates, ING analysts said in a note. The loss of supply would mean higher prices over the longer-term.
The fuels market has become considerably tighter as the war progresses. The easy-to-access oil that was stored on ships is being used while strategic reserves have been drawn down.

Hopes that increasing oil flows coming out of the Middle East would help alleviate some of the pressure were dented after an attack last week on a crucial crude pipeline in Saudi Arabia that helped bypass the Strait of Hormuz. This has stranded at least 2.5 million barrels a day, analysts estimate.
A Russian ban on diesel exports following Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries has added to the lost volumes.

Diesel is a key part of the global economy, fueling trucks that move food and manufactured goods, heavy equipment at construction sites and ships at sea. It is also widely used for heating. A prolonged supply crunch can ripple through the economy, pushing up freight rates and the cost of food, construction and household fuel.
